calendar.action: 19 Oct Life Sciences; 20 Oct CISE, Materials Research, Psychology, Social Sciences; 22 Oct Engineering; 23 Oct Chemistry, Geosciences, Mathematical Sciences, Physics and Astronomy. Do not read the date off the /funding/opportunities landing page — its table renders misaligned and produces a non-existent 26 October date. Use the solicitation (NSF 26-526) or the applicant fact sheet. Official undergraduate transcripts are required and are the slow item. If you decide not to submit, WITHDRAW by 15 Nov 2026 so the attempt does not consume your single graduate-student application.

calendar.window: Tue 27 October 2026, 11:59 PM ET — HHMI Gilliam Fellows
calendar.action: Second- or third-year PhD students only, by total program years, no exceptions. Add your advisor and reference in the ARC portal FIRST — their materials must be in before your application counts as complete, and you are explicitly responsible for reminding them. Strip every journal name from every document, including papers in preparation; cite as 'Full author list. Title of article. (Year) PMID' or DOI. Holding an NSF GRFP or NIH F31 does not bar you from applying.

calendar.window: Wed 28 October 2026, 5:00 PM ET — Mellon/ACLS Dissertation Innovation and Luce/ACLS American Art
calendar.action: Both through ofa.acls.org, both with the reference letter and the institutional statement due at the same hour. Your referee cannot log in until you have entered them, so the real personal deadline was weeks ago — enter them now. Different formats: Mellon/ACLS is 7 pages double-spaced; Luce is 8 pages double-spaced INCLUDING all images and notes with a minimum of three images. The institutional statement writer must not be one of your two Luce letter writers.

calendar.window: Fri 30 October 2026 — NDSEG (5:00 PM ET), Hertz, DAAD Research Grants (midnight CET = 6:00 PM EST)
calendar.action: Three unrelated mechanisms on one day. NDSEG: upload both redacted and original versions of your CV and proposal; redaction extends to publication venues and award names. Hertz: your four recommenders have until 6:00 PM Pacific on 1–2 November (the funder's two pages disagree — treat Sunday 1 Nov as the working deadline) and late references are not accepted. DAAD: you lose the evening of the deadline day, and you must use the North America checklist's 5-page proposal limit, not the Bonn site's 10.

calendar.window: Late October 2026 — DOE CSGF application opens
calendar.action: 'The 2027-2028 application will be available late October 2026' (krellinst.org/doecsgf/application). Eligible only if you have completed no more than one year of full-time graduate work toward the PhD. The application is 16 sections you can complete across multiple visits. The hardest component is the Program of Study — a course table across three areas plus one HPC course — and Krell publishes a worked sample POS. Start it now, not in January. Watch the FAQ page: it still shows the closed 2026 cycle's dates and updates when the application opens.

calendar.window: Wed 4 November 2026, 5:00 PM ET — DOE SCGSR 2026 Solicitation 2
calendar.action: The single best value on this calendar if you are a PhD candidate: a 3-page proposal for a residency at a national lab. The deadline includes all letters of support, and the system closes — nothing is accepted after. Your two 'letters' are structured questionnaire forms, so tell your thesis advisor and the collaborating lab scientist they are answering 4–6 prompts, not drafting prose. Scrub SSN and date of birth from transcripts or you are eliminated automatically. Notification 1–16 April 2027; start June–October 2027.

calendar.window: November–December 2026 — build the NIH fellowship
calendar.action: If you are ABD in the biomedical, behavioral or clinical sciences, the F31 (or F30 for MD/PhD) is the centre of your winter. Registration and eRA Commons setup can take six weeks or more — start immediately. Three to five reference letters go through the eRA Commons Submit Reference Letter link, NOT Grants.gov, and your sponsor cannot be one of the three. Confirm your institution's internal deadline with the sponsored research office: they submit, not you, and it typically runs 3–5 business days early. F30 applicants: verify whether your institution holds an NIH-funded dual-degree program and pick PA-25-426 or PA-25-425 accordingly.

calendar.window: Tue 8 December 2026, 5:00 PM local time of your institution — NIH F31 and F30
calendar.action: Hard. Fellowships are on NIH's excluded list for late submission (NOT-OD-26-064), so there is no grace of any kind. Review March 2027, council May 2027, earliest start July 2027 — about seven months. New and resubmission share this date; there is no one-month offset for A1 as there is for R and K awards. If you miss it, the next dates are 8 April 2027, 8 August 2027, 8 December 2027 and 8 April 2028.

calendar.window: January 2027 — the new-year openings, and the watch list turning over
calendar.action: SfN Neuroscience Scholars Program opens (closed at noon Eastern on Friday 13 Feb last cycle). AGU Horton's window opens in the first week of January. DOE CSGF closes mid-January by pattern (2026 cycle: 15 Jan, letters +1 week, transcripts +2 weeks). NASA expects FINESST-25 decisions in January 2027, and the next FINESST NOFO is gated on them — start watching go.nasa.gov/FINESST25. USDA's FY27 AFRI NOFO should post around late January (FY26 posted 20 Jan with a 16 April predoc deadline). Re-check AGU's Horton page weekly; if it still reads '5 January – 13 March' in late December, email researchgrants@agu.org rather than assuming.

calendar.window: February 2027 — RSF, ASME, SfN
calendar.action: RSF Dissertation Research Grants: the exact day should be posted mid-to-late November 2026 and the portal opens early December; plan against 1–4 February at 2:00 PM ET, treat the first Tuesday (2 Feb) as the modal guess and 1 Feb as the conservative floor. Allow five business days for RSF account approval. ASME Graduate Teaching Fellowship: 15 February 2027 is a Monday and Presidents' Day — submit one complete PDF by email on Friday 12 February; note the department-head certification that appears on the application form but not the web page. SfN NSP closes mid-February at noon Eastern.

calendar.window: March–April 2027 — the second wave
calendar.action: AGU Horton closes mid-March (plan Fri 12 Mar). ACM SIGHPC opens 15 March and closes 30 April — but only one nomination per department, so approach your department head in February, not April. Google PhD Fellowship is projected 5 March – 30 April with campus internal deadlines 2–6 weeks earlier (ask your fellowships office in January). NIH F31/F30 on 8 April. NSF INTERN's annual target is 15 April, though the real constraint is your internship start minus two months. AFRI A7101 expected in the second half of April. DAAD's spring round closes 30 April. NSF CyberAI SFS institutional Innovation Track target is 5 April 2027 — irrelevant to you directly, but it tells you which campuses will be recruiting scholars.

calendar.window: April–August 2027 — decisions land and you choose
calendar.action: GRFP notifies by early April; Gilliam in Summer 2027; SCGSR 1–16 April; RSF about three to four months after its February deadline (observed: announced 18 June in both 2025 and 2026). This is when concurrency actually matters. If you hold two offers: NDSEG is non-deferrable so it is choose-one; Gilliam allows a single one-year deferral if you request it AT notification and HHMI approves; CSGF cannot be held with another federal fellowship; GRFP Reserve status is the mechanism for a year on another award. Get the numbers side by side before you answer anything — Hertz's coordinated option pays $9,000/yr during another award's years, not a second full stipend.

calendar.window: May–August 2027 — set up next year while everyone else is on holiday
calendar.action: May–June: ask your graduate school's fellowships or limited-submission office whether your institution is on Apple's invited list and when the internal call opens (calls went out late June to mid July in 2026; internal deadlines 21 July – 3 August). Ask your advisor whether they hold an IBM nomination invitation. July: IEEE EDS PhD Fellowship closes 15 July by pattern — your EDS-member faculty sponsor nominates and only one candidate per institution can win, so settle that internally in May. Early August: NDSEG and Hertz reopen. Mid-August: FINESST FIs who have heard nothing should ask their PI to log into NSPIRES — NASA will not tell you directly. Mid-October to early December: ASM travel award for ASM Microbe 2027, with abstracts opening mid-November.

calendar.window: Any time, all year — the rolling mechanisms nobody uses
calendar.action: NSF INTERN/GRIP: your PI submits whenever, the AOR signs at least two months before you need the funds, up to $55,000 per six-month period, two per grant per student, host must be non-academic. NIST PREP Gaithersburg: 200 live postings, no deadlines at all. NIST PREP Boulder: set a saved search on jobs.colorado.edu. These have no cycle to miss, which is exactly why they get forgotten — put a standing quarterly reminder on them instead of a deadline.

first_moves: DAY 1 — Write down your matriculation date and count program years from it. Not lab-entry, not candidacy. Gilliam, CSGF, NDSEG, Hertz and GRFP all gate on this number and several state outright that switching labs does not reset it. Then write down your citizenship/status. Those two facts eliminate or unlock roughly two-thirds of this list in ten minutes.

DAY 1–2 — Ask for letters before you write a word. Email the two or three people you will ask, with the list of deadlines, the earliest date, and an offer to send them a one-page summary of what you want each letter to say. For GRFP the letter date (16 Oct 2026, 8:00 PM ET) precedes every applicant date; for SCGSR the letters close inside the same 5:00 PM instant as the application; for Hertz and NVIDIA late letters are simply not accepted. This is the most common way a cycle is lost and it is entirely preventable.

DAY 2 — Find your gatekeeper for each thing you want. For F31/F30, that is the sponsored research office (they submit; ask for their internal deadline, usually 3–5 business days early). For FINESST and INTERN, your PI. For Google, Apple, IBM, IEEE EDS and ACM SIGHPC, a nominating faculty member or department head plus your graduate school's fellowships / limited-submission office. For Knauss, your state Sea Grant program. For CyberAI SFS, the participating campus itself — OPM's own instruction is 'Just send an email asking for availability and application instructions.' Put their names in a single file.

DAY 3 — Order official undergraduate transcripts. GRFP requires them, AGU Horton requires a complete set of graduate transcripts, DOE CSGF requires officials sent directly by the institution and will not accept ones you forward yourself, and SCGSR requires them with SSN and date of birth removed. This is the slowest thing on the list and it is free to start now.

DAY 3–4 — Register everywhere that takes time. ORCID (five minutes, but ACLS expects it). eRA Commons if you are going near NIH — the NOFO warns registration 'can take 6 weeks or more.' NSPIRES if you are a FINESST Future Investigator, because every listed team member must log in and confirm their role or the proposal cannot be submitted. ACLS OFA. RSF's Fluxx (allow five business days for account approval). AGU student membership if you want Horton; ASM membership if you want the travel award; IEEE EDS student membership if you want the fellowship — all three are eligibility conditions, not formalities.

DAY 5 — Draft ONE two-to-three page research statement. Almost everything at this stage is a variation on it: Gilliam wants 3 pages including figures, NVIDIA 2 pages plus bibliography, Apple 4 pages including citations, Google 3 pages excluding references, GRFP 2 pages, SCGSR 3 pages excluding references. Write the fullest version first and cut down, never the reverse. Keep the figures separable so you can drop them when the limit includes them.

DAY 6–7 — Read two funded examples in your own field before you revise. DOE SCGSR's workshop deck has an annotated sample abstract followed by a slide headed 'A More Polished Version' — a real before-and-after. ACLS publishes a complete 48-page screen-by-screen sample application for the Dissertation Innovation Fellowship. RSF publishes two full funded DRG proposals plus the blank form. NASA publishes funded FINESST abstracts by division with the PI–FI pair named. Reading one of these is worth more than a week of drafting blind.

WEEK 2, DAY 1 — Book a conversation with the two or three people who can actually change your odds: your advisor (about which mechanism fits and whether they have nomination invitations), one recent awardee in your subfield, and the fellowships office. Specific questions are in 'who to talk to' below.

WEEK 2, MID-WEEK — Set the watch list, because a third of these have no published next date. Build eight browser bookmarks or calendar reminders: NASA FINESST (go.nasa.gov/FINESST25, from January 2027), AGU Horton (weekly from 1 Dec 2026), RSF deadlines page (mid-November 2026), AHA funding opportunities (early March 2027), NIJ 'Be the first to know' signup, Knauss via your state program (from March 2027), NVIDIA's graduate-fellowships page (from July), and USDA NIFA's AFRI deadlines page (late January 2027). A watch instruction is the correct answer where no date exists; an invented date is not.

WEEK 2, END — Pick your relay, not your application. Write one line for each of the next three years: which mechanism is your primary target, which is the backup, and which window closes permanently at the end of that year. If you are in year 1, GRFP and CSGF and Hertz close forever soon and Gilliam opens next year. If you are in year 3, the early-career fellowships are gone and your money is F31, SCGSR, dissertation fellowships and society grants. Knowing which door is closing is more valuable than any single draft.
who_to_talk_to: YOUR DISSERTATION ADVISOR — first conversation, this week, before you draft anything. Ask three things specifically: (1) Do you hold a nomination invitation for IBM, or is our department on Apple's invited list? Those are invitation-only and a student cannot find out any other way. (2) Do you hold an active NSF award that supports me? That is the entry ticket for an INTERN supplement, and it is the PI who submits it. (3) For Gilliam specifically: are you willing to do the year-long mentorship course (monthly webinars Oct 2027 – Mar 2028 plus an in-person workshop in Spring 2028)? The advisor's commitment is a real cost and it is better asked than assumed.

YOUR DEPARTMENT'S GRADUATE PROGRAM DIRECTOR OR CHAIR — within the first two weeks. Ask: Does this department hold an NIH T32 or an NSF training grant, and how does one get appointed to it? A T32 slot is the easiest predoctoral money in the system because your own program administers it, but it counts against the same five-year NRSA aggregate cap as an F31, so you need to know before you plan. Also ask the ACM SIGHPC question in February, not April: only ONE nomination per department is permitted and the nominator must coordinate with the department head, so the internal decision is the competition.

THE GRADUATE SCHOOL'S FELLOWSHIPS / LIMITED-SUBMISSION OFFICE — contact in May–June for the following year's industry cycles, and immediately if you are looking at anything nominated. This office holds the internal deadlines nobody publishes: Google's campus deadline runs 2–6 weeks before Google's own (Emory 17 April 2026; Colorado School of Mines 15 March 2027; UW runs a three-stage funnel), and Apple's ran 21 July – 3 August 2026 against Apple's 8 September. Named examples of what this office is called: fellowshipLSO@umich.edu, trainee-funding@purdue.edu (which also offers a Fellowship Writing Coach), gsas-fwc@fas.harvard.edu. Ask: which fellowships is this institution invited to, when does the internal call open, and do you offer proposal review?

THE SPONSORED RESEARCH OFFICE / AUTHORIZED ORGANIZATIONAL REPRESENTATIVE — at least six weeks before any NIH deadline. They submit your F31 or F30; you cannot. Ask for their internal cut-off (typically 3–5 business days before NIH's 5:00 PM local deadline), whether your eRA Commons account is active, and whether registration is complete. For NSF INTERN, the AOR must electronically sign in Research.gov at least two months before you need the funds — tell them the internship start date, not the April target date.

THE PROGRAM OFFICER — before you write, not after you are rejected, and only where the funder invites it. NSF INTERN: contacting your cognizant program director is required under NSF 24-071, NSF 24-087 and NSF 23-112, and strongly advised under the parent DCL — that PO is also the only person who can tell your PI what a fundable two-page summary looks like. RSF: 'reach out at least one month ahead of the deadline to programs@rsage.org with a short abstract and some details about the research design.' NIH: for T32-adjacent questions, contact the IC's training officer about which council round takes your application. NIA: 'If you would like feedback on whether your research area is appropriate for the NIA, please include a one-page summary of your Specific Aims.' AFRI A7101: nifafellows@usda.gov. AGU: researchgrants@agu.org. Hertz: fellowshipinfo@hertzfoundation.org. Apple (eligibility only): aiml_scholars@apple.com. IBM: phdfellow@us.ibm.com. DAAD, by contrast, says after submission 'Please DO NOT CALL OR EMAIL' — respect the difference.

A RECENT AWARDEE IN YOUR SUBFIELD — this is the highest-yield hour you will spend, and the rosters to find them in are published. NASA FINESST publishes funded abstracts by division naming the PI–FI pair. NAEd/Spencer publishes every awardee with project title, abstract, institution and discipline at naeducation.org/awardees/. AGU publishes 98 Horton recipients filterable by year, section and career stage. SfN publishes the named NSP cohort with institution and research area. NVIDIA, Google, Apple and IBM publish recipient lists. Ask them: what did the reviewers push back on, how long did it actually take, and what would you do differently? Ask in the month the cycle opens, when it is fresh in their mind.

YOUR STATE SEA GRANT PROGRAM DIRECTOR — now, if you are anywhere near marine, coastal, Great Lakes or ocean policy. You never apply to NOAA; your state program runs the round that filters you and then submits on your behalf. Their deadline is the one that binds (1 July for the 2027 class) and no 2028 date exists yet. Ask what their internal review looks like and what they want to see by spring.

THE HOST-SIDE COLLABORATOR, for placement-based awards — this is a relationship, not a form. SCGSR requires a named DOE laboratory scientist who will complete a questionnaire for you, and you must not already have spent three months working at that lab. NSF INTERN requires a non-academic host who signs a letter of collaboration AND agrees an IP arrangement in advance. Start these conversations three to four months out; they are the long pole. Note the exception: for Knauss, contacting a prospective federal host office before placement week is grounds for immediate disqualification.

YOUR INSTITUTION'S IRB OFFICE — early, if you are doing human-subjects work. NIJ will not release funds until an IRB determination and Privacy Certificate are submitted and approved. RSF requires IRB approval or exemption at the due-diligence stage after positive external review. These take weeks and cannot be compressed.
materials_to_gather: A SINGLE MASTER RESEARCH STATEMENT, 3–4 pages, written long and cut down. Every mechanism is a trim of it: Gilliam 3 pages including figures with citations separate; Apple 4 pages including citations; Google 3 pages excluding references; NVIDIA 2 pages with the bibliography excluded; GRFP 2 pages; SCGSR 3 pages excluding references (references capped at 1 page); Mellon/ACLS 7 pages double-spaced; Luce/ACLS 8 pages double-spaced including ALL images and notes; RSF 5 pages single-spaced; NAEd/Spencer 10 pages double-spaced; NIJ 8 pages; DAAD 5 pages (North America checklist, which supersedes the Bonn site's 10); FINESST 6 pages excluding citations. Keep figures in a separate file so you can drop them where the limit swallows them.

A PERSONAL / CAREER STATEMENT, and treat it as a distinct genre from the research statement. GRFP's is 3 pages and carries as much weight as the 2-page research plan. Gilliam wants a career statement plus leadership statements plus a conflict-resolution statement co-written with your advisor. Hertz wants a 500–1000-word personal essay and several 250–500-word short essays. NDSEG wants a 500-word personal essay. SfN wants a 500-word two-year plan and a 500-word goals statement. ASM wants 500 words. Write the long version once.

OFFICIAL TRANSCRIPTS — the slowest item on the list and free to start today. GRFP requires official undergraduate transcripts. AGU Horton requires a complete set of graduate transcripts. DOE CSGF requires officials sent DIRECTLY by the university ('Transcripts sent by an applicant will not be accepted') by 31 January. SCGSR requires them with SSN and date of birth removed or the application is auto-eliminated. NIJ requires undergraduate AND graduate. Hertz, NAEd/Spencer and SfN accept unofficial at the application stage. Gilliam and Fulbright-era ACLS do not require them at all.

REFERENCE LETTERS — the binding constraint of the entire year, and the thing to manage like a project. Counts vary: GRFP three named (up to five listed), Gilliam one advisor letter plus one reference, Hertz four, NVIDIA two to three including the thesis advisor, NIH F31 three to five with the sponsor not counting toward the three, Luce/ACLS two with one from the dissertation advisor, ASM two on institutional letterhead from the department chair AND the PI, IEEE EDS two that cannot come from the nominator, AGU Horton two (research supervisor plus another committee member, on letterhead, signed, filename 'Applicant Last Name_Referee Last Name'), NDSEG up to three, optional, on letterhead NOT accepted. Give writers a one-page brief and the deadline with its clock time. SCGSR's 'letters' are questionnaire FORMS (4 topics for the advisor, 5–6 for the lab scientist) — tell them so they don't draft prose.

A BIOSKETCH IN TWO FORMATS. NIH SciENcv biosketch for F31/F30 and T32; a plain 2–3 page academic CV for everything else. Length limits differ sharply: DAAD 3 pages, Knauss 2 pages with no personal contact info and no web links, Luce/ACLS and Mellon/ACLS via their own templates, ACM SIGHPC's candidate CV must list all degrees, the FULL publication list, leadership and service, and awards, RSF 5 pages, IBM 3 pages, ASME resume or vitae with no stated limit. Also keep a separate current-and-pending-support list: FINESST requires you to list concurrent GRFP and NSTGRO applications there, and Knauss's state program discloses your fellowships and internships on your behalf.

YOUR ADVISOR'S MATERIALS, which are not yours and take their calendar time. Gilliam needs six components from them plus a co-written conflict-resolution statement. AHA's predoctoral fellowship weights the mentor at 40% and needs their biosketch, a 3-page past-and-current-trainees list, a 3-page training plan and a research environment statement. Google needs a 1-page advisor CV and a chair-signed cover sheet. NIH needs a full sponsor and co-sponsor section. SfN needs the adviser's biosketch. Ask six weeks out, not two.

A BUDGET AND ITS JUSTIFICATION, where one is required — and note that it usually is not at this stage. AGU Horton needs an itemised budget with travel broken into transportation, hotel/per diem and registration. NSF INTERN needs a budget with clear justification. AFRI A7101 is capped at $180,000 total / $60,000 per year (up to $35,000 stipend, $22,000 other, $3,000 institutional allowance) with indirect costs not permitted, and 'requests exceeding budgetary guidelines will not be reviewed.' NIJ has a budget detail form. By contrast GRFP, Gilliam, NDSEG, Hertz and the ACLS fellowships need no budget at all, and RSF does not ask for one until after positive external review.

PROOF OF CANDIDACY OR ENROLLMENT, which is a hard gate more often than people expect. SCGSR needs a letter confirming PhD candidacy. AFRI A7101 requires you to have ADVANCED TO CANDIDACY by the application deadline itself, with documentation from the advisor or institution filed by then. RSF requires ABD status ('completed all program requirements except the dissertation'). Luce/ACLS requires ABD before tenure begins and the entire fellowship term must conclude before the PhD is conferred. NIJ requires a Verification of Current Enrollment. NAEd/Spencer requires pre-dissertation requirements complete by 1 June 2027. Get the letter your graduate school issues for this and keep a signed PDF.

MEMBERSHIPS AND REGISTRATIONS THAT ARE ELIGIBILITY CONDITIONS, NOT FORMALITIES. AGU student membership (required to apply for Horton, and you must stay enrolled for a year from the annual meeting where the award is presented). ASM membership at application AND through the meeting. IEEE EDS student membership at the time of nomination, with an EDS-member sponsor. ASME student membership plus an ABET-accredited undergraduate degree. Buy these before the window opens, not during it.

AN IP AGREEMENT AND A HOST LETTER, for placement awards. NSF INTERN requires 'a signed agreement on IP (including publication and patent rights)' between your NSF awardee institution and the non-academic host before the supplement can be awarded — this passes through two legal offices and is the longest lead item in that mechanism. SCGSR requires a named DOE lab scientist who completes a form for you.

A PLAIN-LANGUAGE SUMMARY, for the funders that demand one and enforce it. AHA will not let you submit if your non-scientist summary reads above the 12th-grade level. FINESST, Gilliam and RSF all reward it even where they do not enforce it. Write it once and reuse.
where_to_find_examples: FULL FUNDED APPLICATIONS — rare, but real in three places. RSF publishes two complete funded Dissertation Research Grant proposals plus the blank form (russellsage.org/sites/default/files/2025-08/sample_drg_proposals.pdf — verified live, 11 pages; the applicant names in it could not be independently confirmed, so read it for structure rather than citing its authors). ACLS publishes a 48-page screen-by-screen print-out of the entire Dissertation Innovation Fellowship application (acls.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/DIF-Sample-Application.pdf) — CAUTION: it is the 2022-23 cycle, every date inside it is dead, use it for screen order and field content only. NIAID publishes full funded F31 applications paired with their summary statements — the only NIH collection verified as F31-specific.

ANNOTATED SAMPLES WITH FUNDER COMMENTARY — the single most useful artefact type, and it exists for exactly one mechanism here. DOE SCGSR's applicant workshop deck carries a slide headed 'Abstract Sample' with reviewer-style callouts (Problem? Approach? Need of lab resources? Outcomes? Connection to thesis) followed immediately by a slide headed 'A More Polished Version...' — a genuine before-and-after from the funder. The preceding slide gives the element checklist the annotations key to.

FUNDED ABSTRACTS BY FIELD, which tell you what wins even when the application text is withheld. NASA FINESST publishes selections per division, alphabetical by PI, naming the PI–FI pair, institution, proposal number and a full abstract — the 2021 cycle published 139 selections from 927 proposals across six divisions. NSF's award search returns live CyberAI SFS abstracts (45 records in 2026) and is browsable per programme. NAEd publishes every awardee at naeducation.org/awardees/ with project title, abstract, institution, discipline and fellowship year — filterable to your own subfield. AHA's reSEARCH@Heart portal (heart.dimensions.ai/discover/grant) shows funded projects, with AHA's own caveat that it is 'best used to look for EXAMPLES of funding, rather than total Association funding on a particular topic.' RSF publishes roughly 100 funded DRG abstracts.

FUNDER-RUN WEBINARS AND INFO SESSIONS, which are the closest thing to being told the rubric. HHMI's 2027 Gilliam information session is recorded and the 23-slide deck is public. NIJ's FY25 pre-application webinar has a recording, a transcript and slides. SCGSR's applicant workshop deck is the source of the annotated abstract above. Fulbright maintains a recorded-webinar library with sessions on the Statement of Grant Purpose, the Short Answers, and finding a Letter of Affiliation (note: there is no Personal Statement webinar). AHA runs live applicant webinars with Q&A and posts recordings. Hertz publishes 'Advice from Hertz Fellows' videos — check the dates, the top item is often last cycle's session.

PUBLISHED RUBRICS AND SCORING WEIGHTS, where the funder prints them. AHA's predoctoral review is weighted 30/40/30 across applicant, mentor/training plan and research — with the mentor half carrying 40% — on a 1–9 scale, and up to half of submissions are streamlined with no comments and no score before review even begins. Fulbright-Hays DDRA published a 100-point rubric in its last notice (methods and questions 20, advisor supervision 10, literature and originality 10 — historical only, since the competition is cancelled). NVIDIA publishes a substantial 'Helpful Hints' section that functions as a rubric, including the instruction to 'Connect your work to NVIDIA.' NSF's PAPPG and each solicitation's review criteria are the equivalent for NSF mechanisms.

BLANK FORMS AND TEMPLATES, which are underrated. AHA publishes a Predoctoral Fellowship biosketch SAMPLE (DOCX) and a Reference Report Form template. DOE CSGF publishes a worked sample Program of Study — a full course table across the three required areas — which is the hardest component for a first-year applicant and the best starter material on that site. RSF publishes its blank application form. ACLS publishes the required one-page timeline template.

RECIPIENT ROSTERS, when nothing else is published — these are for finding PEOPLE, not text. NVIDIA explicitly tells applicants to calibrate against them: 'We suggest you look at the list of past recipients and see whether your application is comparable.' AGU lists 98 Horton recipients filterable by year, section, region and career stage. SfN publishes its named NSP cohort with institution and research area. Apple, Google and IBM publish names. IEEE EDS goes further — the January EDS Newsletter (free, no login) reprints the full call for nominations AND carries multi-page technical profiles of the previous year's PhD Fellows describing the work that won, which is the closest published proxy for a winning research statement in that programme.

PROJECT AND POSITION ARCHIVES, for learning house style. NIST PREP's prep.umd.edu lists roughly 200 project postings with sponsor name, research summary, position category and start date — the richest public picture of what NIST sponsors actually ask for. Treat it as a corpus of examples, not a vacancy board; apply through a hub's live system. Harvard's Apple Scholars page reproduces all 13 Apple research areas with Apple's own definitions and sub-topic lists — the best public artefact for deciding which two areas to rank, since Apple's own guide is closed.

HONEST NEGATIVES — say these plainly rather than implying material exists. No sample application, annotated example or successful narrative is published for: NDSEG, DOE CSGF (funded application texts; the POS sample does exist), AFRI A7101, NSF GRFP essays (NSF hosts templates and the awardee roster; real essays circulate only through the community), ACM SIGHPC, IEEE EDS, ASM, ASME GTF, SfN NSP, AGU Horton, Apple, Google, IBM, NVIDIA, DAAD, Knauss, NIJ, Luce/ACLS, HHMI Gilliam, CIRM, NIST PREP, and NSF INTERN. NIH's own curated samples index does not carry an F30. HHMI states it cannot provide individual feedback on applications; DAAD states decisions come without explanation; ACLS will provide reviewer comments only on request and at each reviewer's discretion, with requests for the 2026-27 competition due by 30 June 2027.
common_mistakes: MISSING THE LETTER DEADLINE RATHER THAN YOUR OWN. NSF GRFP references close 16 Oct 2026 at 8:00 PM ET — three days before the earliest applicant deadline and seven before the latest — and fewer than two received means the application is not reviewed. SCGSR's deadline includes all letters and the system then closes entirely. NVIDIA's letters close at 12 noon PT, three hours before the 3:00 PM PT student deadline. Hertz does not accept late references at all. Gilliam will not treat your application as complete until your advisor and reference have submitted, and HHMI says explicitly that reminding them is your job.

COUNTING PROGRAM YEARS FROM THE WRONG DATE. Gilliam counts total years in the graduate program, not years in the thesis lab, and states that switching labs 'does not reset or extend program year eligibility' — then answers the exceptions question with a flat 'No.' DOE CSGF disqualifies anyone who has completed more than one year of full-time graduate work. NDSEG needs you within the first two years AND with at least three years remaining, so a fifth-year is out on both ends. Apple wants students entering their last two to three years and states G1s are not eligible. Get this number right before you spend a week writing.

ASSUMING A CONCURRENT AWARD DISQUALIFIES YOU FROM APPLYING. It almost never does. Gilliam's conflict bites at activation (relinquish or request a one-year deferral approved by HHMI at notification). NDSEG has no prior-award question in its eligibility screener at all. FINESST explicitly permits concurrent GRFP and NSTGRO applications provided you list them as current and pending. Google's bar is on 'comparable industry award' only, with government and non-profit funding exempt. Self-rejecting on a rule that applies at acceptance costs a whole cycle for nothing.

MISSING THE INSTITUTIONAL PRE-STAGE, WHICH IS USUALLY THE REAL COMPETITION. Google's campus nomination deadlines ran 2–6 weeks before Google's 30 April close. Apple's internal competitions ran 21 July – 3 August against Apple's 8 September, with calls posted late June. ACM SIGHPC permits one nomination per department. IEEE EDS allows only one winner per institution. Fulbright campus deadlines run 4–6 weeks before the national date. DAAD's partner-university pre-selection exists only for the fall deadline. None of these are advertised the way the funder's own date is, and by the time you see the funder's deadline you have already lost.

TRUSTING THE AGGREGATOR OR THE LANDING PAGE INSTEAD OF THE SOLICITATION. Grants.gov shows 31 December 2026 for USDA's AFRI EWD NOFO — that is an umbrella placeholder for continuously-accepted workshop grants, eight months past the real A7101 predoctoral date. A plain fetch of NSF's GRFP landing page returns a misaligned table that invents a non-existent 26 October deadline. Knauss's own FAQ currently prints '3 June 2026' as the application deadline, which is actually the enrolment cut-off pasted into the wrong answer, four weeks before the real 1 July date. Read the NOFO or solicitation, not the summary.

READING A STALE PAGE AS A LIVE ONE, OR AS EVIDENCE A PROGRAMME ENDED. AGU's Horton page today shows an undated '5 January – 13 March' window that is the already-closed 2026 cycle — AGU leaves closed windows on display for months. RSF's own RFP still carries the 3 February 2026 deadline. NVIDIA's page still shows September 2025. IBM describes its 2025 cycle in the future tense with awardees listed only to 2024. UC Irvine's CIRM page still shows a June 2024 deadline. None of this means the programme is dead; it means you check the date stamp and, where there is no stamp, email the address the funder publishes.

APPLYING TO A MECHANISM THAT IS NOT FOR YOU. ARPA-E's IGNIITE requires a pre-tenure Tenure-Track Assistant or Associate Professor and bars co-PIs outright — it is a faculty award, and its FAQ says exceptions will not be considered. CIRM Bridges, COMPASS and SPARK are undergraduate, master's and high-school programmes. NIH T32 and NSF CyberAI SFS are grants to institutions, not applications you file. Fulbright-Hays DDRA was cancelled on 9 May 2025 and has made zero awards since FY2024.

OVERSHOOTING OR UNDERSHOOTING A PAGE LIMIT BECAUSE YOU REUSED THE WRONG ONE. Harvard's internal Apple statement is two pages; Apple's own is four. DAAD's Bonn site says 10 pages; the North America checklist says 5 and explicitly supersedes it. ACM SIGHPC's prose page says 300 characters for two nominator fields; the live form enforces 200 on one of them, and says 1000 for a candidate statement its prose page describes as 500. Luce/ACLS counts images and notes inside its 8 pages; Mellon/ACLS excludes citations from its 7; Gilliam includes figures in its 3 but excludes citations. AGU removes excess pages before review. ACLS excludes non-conforming applications from review outright.

INCLUDING SOMETHING THE FUNDER DID NOT ASK FOR. NASA FINESST: letters of mentorship or recommendation from a NASA Research Center are not allowed, and 'Including such letters or other documents FINESST does not request can lead to your proposal being returned without review for non-compliance.' FINESST also says 'No additional components or files are permitted,' which means a response-to-reviewers document is itself a compliance violation. HHMI forbids journal names anywhere in the application, including for papers in preparation. Apple asks you to redact date of birth, PII and photographs. SCGSR eliminates transcripts carrying an SSN or date of birth.

TREATING A RESUBMISSION AS A CONTINUATION WHEN THE FUNDER TREATS IT AS NEW. NASA: 'Each submission to FINESST, including a resubmission, is considered to be an ENTIRELY new proposal. NASA does not compare prior and current year proposals,' and NASA warns that addressing last year's reviewers 'may confuse the new reviewers.' RSF: a revised application 'will be processed as a new submission.' SCGSR: 'Your application will only be kept on record for the current application period.' Conversely, NIH and AHA DO track it — NIH allows a single A1 within 37 months and forbids submitting it before the A0 summary statement issues; AHA assigns a resubmission to at least one prior reviewer and gives reviewers your previous critiques and scores. Know which regime you are in.

BURNING A ONE-SHOT ATTEMPT. NSF GRFP allows a graduate student a single application — the 15 November 2026 withdrawal date exists so a withdrawn attempt does not consume it, so withdraw rather than submit something weak. Luce/ACLS permits exactly one reapplication and makes it an eligibility gate, not a norm. RSF has a lifetime limit of one DRG per person. Knauss bars anyone who has been accepted as a national finalist from reapplying without written permission. ASM starts a two-year clock across its whole travel-award family, not just the one you won.

FORGETTING THAT THE AWARD HAS CONDITIONS THAT OUTLAST THE APPLICATION. NVIDIA's summer internship is mandatory and in person. IEEE EDS requires you to stay at the same institution with the same advisor for twelve months after the award. IBM requires you to stay in the same program. AGU Horton requires enrolment for a year from the annual meeting where the award is presented, which catches anyone defending mid-award. Gilliam obliges your advisor to a year-long mentorship course, and obliges you to HHMI programming even if you defer activation. Knauss requires relocation to Washington DC and passing a federal background check. ASM reimburses travel AFTER the meeting, about six months after you are told you won — you front the cost.

WAITING FOR A DECISION THROUGH THE WRONG CHANNEL. NASA FINESST Future Investigators cannot see decisions or review results in NSPIRES at all — 'If by August 15, the PI or AOR have not contacted the FI, then the FI should ask them to log in.' NIFA warns that if your Authorized Representative has not heard from them within 30 days of the deadline, you must contact the programme or 'the application not being considered for funding by the peer review panel.' Know who receives the notification and calendar the chase.

result.career_stage: Postdoc (United States) — including international postdocs in US labs and US-trained postdocs applying to non-US funders
result.narrative:
ON THE DATED-DEADLINE QUESTION, FIRST, BECAUSE IT SHAPES EVERYTHING BELOW. Nothing forbids a dated deadline, and stripping dates would gut this page — a postdoc who is told only "annual, see the NOFO" cannot decide whether to start writing in October or next June. The rule that actually holds up under verification is "no UNDATED dates": every date below is shown with the funder page it came from and the day it was read (2026-09-18), past cycles are marked CLOSED rather than deleted, and anything not published by the funder is labelled PROJECTED and never dressed up as a deadline. Where a funder genuinely has not posted the next date, this says so. That is not evasion — for several mechanisms (USDA AFRI postdoc fellowships, ARPA-E IGNIITE, APS Blewett) the programme is alive and the DATE is the thing that rots, so the honest artifact is a stamped date plus a watch route.

WHAT A POSTDOC IS ACTUALLY PLAYING FOR. There are three different games and they have different logics. (1) PORTABLE SALARY FELLOWSHIPS pay you for 2–3 years and make you cheaper to hire: NIH F32, NSF PRFB / AAPF / MSPRF, NASA NPP, EMBO, HFSP, Damon Runyon, AHA, and the disease foundations (Breakthrough T1D, CFF, ALS/Safenowitz, Alzheimer's AARFA, Blood Cancer United CDP Fellow, ADA, MSCRF, NJCCR, TRDRP). (2) CAREER-TRANSITION AWARDS buy independence by funding the tail of your postdoc and the first years of a faculty lab: NIH K99/R00, BWF CASI, HHMI Hanna H. Gray, Schmidt Science Fellows. These are the ones that change your job market, and they are the ones with clocks. (3) LAYERS that don't compete with either and are badly under-used: the NIH Loan Repayment Program (up to a two-year contract, no NIH grant required, OPEN NOW and closing 19 November 2026, 11:59 p.m. EST), BWF's Postdoctoral Enrichment Program (a career-development supplement that REQUIRES you to already have a funded postdoc), society travel awards (ASM, SfN NSP), and re-entry supplements for people coming back after a 6-month-to-8-year interruption.

THE FIRST SORT IS CITIZENSHIP, NOT SCIENCE. The NIH F32 requires US citizenship, non-citizen national status, or lawful permanent residence by time of award (verbatim in PA-25-423). So do NSF PRFB ("Must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, or U.S. permanent resident... at the time of submission") and NSF AAPF. So does the USDA AFRI postdoc fellowship, and so does the LRP. If you are on a visa, those are closed and it is not worth a day of your time — but K99/R00 (whose verified disqualifier list is about independence and the 4-year clock, not citizenship — confirm with the IC before you build on it), EMBO, HFSP, Damon Runyon, AHA, HHMI Hanna Gray, Schmidt, most disease foundations, and CIRM's California stem-cell programmes (UCSF, verbatim: "There are no citizenship requirements") are all open. Get this settled in week one; it halves the list either way.

F32 VS K99 — THE DECISION, AND WHY THE K99 CLOCK IS THE MOST IMPORTANT DATE IN YOUR POSTDOC. The F32 funds you as a trainee: three cycles a year (8 April / 8 August / 8 December, 5 p.m. local time of the applicant organisation), a hard 3-year aggregate cap on NRSA support at the postdoctoral level that INCLUDES any T32 time you have already used, and a package built around a 6-page Research Training Project Strategy plus a 6-page sponsor statement. The K99/R00 funds your exit: 1–2 mentored years plus up to 3 independent years you carry to your first faculty job. Its gate is verbatim: "no more than 4 years of related postdoctoral research training at the time of initial application OR RESUBMISSION." Read that twice. The clock does not stop for the A1. You get one resubmission, the A1 cannot be filed before the A0's summary statement issues (roughly 5 months), and that sequencing is what forces an October A0 into a JULY A1 rather than March. So an A0 filed at 46 months is effectively a single shot. The planning rule is to aim your A0 at roughly 24–36 months of postdoc so a real A1 still lands inside the window. Two published softeners: NIH grants an automatic one-year extension for childbirth, but the justification must reach IC programme staff at least 12 weeks before you submit; and leave under 12 months, clinical training with no research, and part-time postdoc work (pro-rated) do not count toward the four years. One hard fact that outranks all of this if you work on cancer: NCI DOES NOT PARTICIPATE in the parent K99/R00 at all (NOT-CA-25-021) — check the participating-IC list before you write a word.

THE SEQUENCING PROBLEM IS BIGGER THAN THE APPLICATION PROBLEM. Almost none of these awards bar you from APPLYING because of what you hold; many bar you from HOLDING two at once, and they adjudicate at the offer. Damon Runyon is the sharp exception and it bites at application: "Candidates who have already accepted a postdoctoral research fellowship award are not eligible," and holding or being awarded an NIH K disqualifies you (institutional K12 may apply but must be turned back). BWF CASI excludes anyone who holds or has accepted a K99 — but explicitly allows K01 holders. ADA's Pathway Initiator bars a concurrent K99/R00 and allows every other career-development award. Blood Cancer United runs a VALUE test (no award of higher total value at the award start date) with an explicit K99 carve-out. Breakthrough T1D and the ALS Safenowitz bar a concurrent postdoctoral fellowship. EMBO and HFSP bar concurrent salaried employment or another paid fellowship but let you top up the living allowance and hold research grants. HHMI says plainly that other funding does not stop you applying and that it reviews arrangements only if you are offered a place. The strategy that follows: apply broadly, never self-reject on funding history, read each award's "what you may HOLD" clause rather than its "who may apply" clause, and decide the order of acceptances deliberately — take the one with the tightest bar first only if you are sure, because accepting a generic postdoc fellowship in year one can close Damon Runyon permanently.

HOW THE YEAR IS ACTUALLY SHAPED. September–October is the federal bottleneck: NSF PRFB (29 Sept 2026), NSF AAPF window close (15 Oct 2026), NSF MSPRF (21 Oct 2026), the NIH K-series new-application date published as 12 October 2026 and operative Tuesday 13 October because 12 October is Columbus Day, and the Blood Cancer United eligibility gate (15 Oct 2026). November–December is the fellowship-and-money month: LRP (19 Nov), NASA NPP (1 Nov), F32 (8 Dec), HHMI Hanna Gray (15 Dec). January–March is foundation season: EMBO's January cutoff, MSCRF and NJCCR in mid-January and early March, Damon Runyon on 15 March 2027. April–July is the second federal round plus the trans-Atlantic and diabetes/T1D cycles. August–September closes the loop with AHA, Pew, BWF CASI's LOI, and the NSF fellowships again. If you are in the humanities or social sciences the shape is different and earlier: ACLS Fellowships close mid-September (the earliest date on the ACLS calendar), Luce/ACLS China Studies Early Career on 5 November 2026, RSF Visiting Researchers on 4 May 2027.

WHAT IS HONESTLY NOT KNOWABLE TODAY. As of 2026-09-18 the following have NO published next date and a projection would be a guess: the FY2028 AHA Postdoctoral Fellowship (expect RFP late April 2027, deadline first week of August 2027 — pattern only); BWF's PDEP (last cycle closed 20 Jan 2026; portal historically opens October); the 2028 Pew Latin American Fellows class (Pew posts new dates on its FAQ between February and May); Simons Junior Fellows 2028 cohort (five consecutive cycles closed 9–15 September at noon ET, so expect that window in 2027); HFSP AY2028; ASM Microbe travel awards for the 2027 meeting (abstracts open mid-November 2026); APS Blewett 2027 (the live page contradicts itself, reading "Nominations are open" and "Nominations are currently closed" simultaneously); the FY2027 USDA AFRI postdoc fellowship (the FY2026 date was 30 April 2026 and the NOFO historically posts January–May — do NOT use the 31 Dec 2026 date on the Grants.gov card, which is the NOFO-wide envelope and is eight months adrift from the A7201 row); and IGNIITE 2027, which does not exist as a posted NOFO — and in any case requires a pre-tenure tenure-track faculty appointment, so it is not a postdoc route.
